title: Why is there an N in "passenger"?

entries.note: Once usual in British English too, but it fell out of use there after becoming the name for the punishment of shipping convicts to the Americas and Australia.
From French, literally to carry across; Britain says public transport where Americans say [[see:transportation]].
Compared with the old punitive sense of [[see:transportation]]; shares the carry root despite seeming linked to [[see:port]].
Like [[same-root:transport]], it comes from the French verb meaning to carry, not from the harbour sense of [[see:port]].
Another carry word sharing a root with [[same-root:transport]], with no etymological link to harbours.
A seaport is linked to the French word for a door, named because things enter there; it ultimately shares a root with [[same-root:transport]].
Originally just a traveller or passer-by; its N was added to the earlier French form simply because English speakers liked the sound.
Centuries younger than [[see:passenger]], apparently coined to fill the gap once passenger narrowed in meaning.
Like [[see:passenger]], it gained an N that its French source lacked.
Another word that picked up an extra N from English speakers, like [[see:passenger]].
Once neutral: someone sent ahead to arrange lodging, or an innkeeper; from a French verb meaning to provide lodging, related to [[same-root:harbor]] and [[same-root:auberge]].
Related to the French lodging word behind [[same-root:harbinger]].
French word the hosts give for a youth hostel, related to [[same-root:harbinger]].
German for a youth hostel; its ending matches the source of [[same-root:harbinger]].
Literally to get onto a bark, a small ship; related to Spanish [[same-root:barca]].
Spanish for a boat, confirmed as related to [[same-root:embark]].
One of the travel words in the episode; it literally means a running out.
Literally an unfettering, from a foot-chain root; first used of making ready for military campaigns; related to [[same-root:expedite]].
Literally to remove the chain from someone's feet, sharing its root with [[same-root:expedition]].
Originally travel by ox-drawn cart, from a Dutch word meaning to draw or pull; related to [[same-root:drag]], [[same-root:draw]], [[same-root:track]] and [[same-root:train]].
Related to [[same-root:trek]].
Related to [[same-root:trek]] and [[same-root:train]].
Named as related to [[same-root:trek]].
Shares a pull or draw root with [[same-root:trek]]; strictly the whole set of vehicles that trails behind the [[see:locomotive]].
The engine that pulls a [[see:train]]; rail enthusiasts insist the two are not the same thing.
Anything that rolls along the rails, a term news writers had to keep separate from [[see:train]] and [[see:locomotive]].
Strictly an engine, not a [[see:train]], except when he has his carriages behind him.
American word for the staffed car at the back of a train; originally a Dutch word for a ship's galley, later slang for the backside.
Flashing rear end device, which has replaced the [[see:caboose]] at the back of trains and signals the driver that the train is intact.
A lover of iron horses, meaning a rail enthusiast, possibly one who likes older trains in particular.
Suggested as the term for a [[see:ferroequinologist]] who specifically loves old trains.
North American term for what Britain calls a [[equivalent:trainspotter]].
British term for enthusiasts who wait by the tracks to spot trains or engines they haven't seen before; the equivalent of a [[equivalent:railfan]].
British nickname for a trainspotter, perhaps a deliberate corruption of [[from?:grouse]]rs, since trainspotters got mistaken for grouse hunters.
Trainspotters were mistaken for grouse hunters, which may explain [[see:gricer]].
US railroads standardised time zones so trains could keep to schedule, since noon varied too much; the zones became official in 1918.
Also called a [[see:truck]], the chassis carrying a rail vehicle's wheels that helps it take curves.
Hinged device on the roof of electric trains and trams that collects power from the overhead wires; Rob shows one on a model tram.
Circular railway building with a turntable; Jess thinks the origin of the name is fairly mundane.
Old railway [[see:roundhouse]] in Rob's hometown, which once hosted an annual beer festival.
Named for the arc of the kick, which looks like a railway [[from:roundhouse]].
Disturbing film whose glossary of strong Edinburgh dialect came up when Rob searched for [[see:trainspotter]] jargon.
Edinburgh dialect for a baby, explained in the [[see:Trainspotting]] glossary.
Slang for a toilet, from the [[see:Trainspotting]] glossary.
Slang for a mate, from the [[see:Trainspotting]] glossary.
Term from the [[see:Trainspotting]] book meaning self-pitying.
[[see:Trainspotting]] slang for being too high on heroin to have sex.
Jess's favourite steam locomotive type, the one you would probably draw if you doodled an engine.
Short for [[from:omnibus]].
Latin for 'for all', the dative of omnis; the name came from a pun on a Nantes hat shop sign, [[from:Omnès Omnibus]], outside a stop on [[see:Stanislas Baudry]]'s route.
Frenchman who in 1823 started a horse-drawn passenger service to his spa; it became the first [[see:omnibus]].
Sign on a Nantes hat shop owned by a Mr Omnès, punning on his name; it gave the [[gave:omnibus]] its name.
What the people of Nantes called Baudry's service, which gave English [[gave:omnibus]].
Perhaps one of the most universal words; named after the [[from:taximeter]], not the vehicle, and related to [[same-root:tax]].
Rob has discussed before how it is a handy multi-purpose word.
Originally a German device that measured distance travelled and the fare owed; from Latin taxa, a tax or tariff, and gave [[gave:taxi]].
Shares its Latin root with [[same-root:taxi]].
A horse for hire, later used for hackney carriages and London black cabs; named after the place [[from:Hackney (place)]].
A private-hire cab, contrasted with a [[see:hackney]] carriage hailed in the street.
A cab for hire that worked around a train depot; the term evolved into [[gave:station wagon]].
Developed from [[from:depot hack]], because these vehicles hung around stations.
London place name, Old English for perhaps Haca's island or hook island, ending in the island suffix [[see:-ey]]; it gave [[gave:hackney]].
A typical island suffix in place names, attributed to the Vikings, as at the end of [[see:Hackney (place)]].
Not short for [[see:carriage]] but older in English; from Latin for a chariot, perhaps via Irish, and long used for any wheeled vehicle.
Came later via French, meaning both the vehicle and the act of transporting; ultimately from the same Latin chariot word as [[same-root:car]].
A [[see:hybrid word]] of Greek auto and Latin-derived mobile, meaning self-mover, so arguably the first self-driving car.
A word mixing two languages, such as [[see:automobile]] and [[see:television]]; supposedly frowned on but very common, and Jess collects them.
Another [[see:hybrid word]], like [[see:automobile]].
Name of the Zoroastrian god of wisdom, chosen because it sounded like the surname of owner [[see:Jujiro Matsuda]].
Owner of the company whose surname resembled [[see:Mazda]].
Japanese name for the [[see:Pleiades]] or Seven Sisters, which appear in the logo; in the US there's a running joke that lesbians drive them.
The Seven Sisters constellation, called [[see:Subaru]] in Japanese.
Loosely means three water chestnuts, reflected in its three-diamond logo.
Short for Nihon Sangyo, Japan Industries, its abbreviation on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
Korean for modernity; its pronunciation varies, and a US ad campaign rhymed it with Sunday.
Korean company with a Chinese-origin name; according to the company, Ki means to arise and A is from Asia, so rising out of Asia.
Latin for listen, translating founder [[from:August Horch]]'s surname, which his former partners' company already used.
Founder of [[see:Audi]]; Horch is German for listen.
Abbreviation of the German for Bavarian Motor Works.
Named after [[from:Antoine Laumet de La Mothe Cadillac]], a figure in New France and the founder of [[see:Detroit]].

entries.term: Antoine Laumet de La Mothe Cadillac
entries.note: A major figure in 17th- and 18th-century New France who founded [[see:Detroit]], and namesake of [[see:Cadillac]].
Founded by the man after whom [[see:Cadillac]] is named, which explains the French name.
Romanian car brand named after an ancient name for Romania.
Abbreviation meaning Swedish aeroplane company, because the firm made planes before cars.
Latin for I roll, related to [[same-root:revolve]].
Rob's clue for working out the meaning of [[same-root:Volvo]].
Possibly apocryphal story that it sold poorly in Spanish-speaking countries because no va means doesn't go.
In French the name is pronounced like merdeux, which roughly means shitty.
One of the rare real acronym origins: GP, general purpose vehicle, probably military slang that became a brand.
The founding family's name goes back to a Dutch word for a lemon, which is funny since a bad car is a [[see:lemon]].
Slang for a bad car, which makes the lemon behind [[see:Citroën]] funny.
The world's first trolleybus-like vehicle, powered from an overhead line through a [[see:pantograph]].
Named because it trolls, meaning strolls or rolls around; unrelated to [[unrelated:troll]] but related to [[same-root:shopping trolley]].
The monster, which is unrelated to [[unrelated:trolley]].
British term for a [[equivalent:shopping cart]], related to [[same-root:trolley]].
American equivalent of the British [[equivalent:shopping trolley]].
Torpedo-like first road vehicle to exceed 100 km/h, driven by [[see:Camille Jenatzy]]; the name boasts of its insatiable need to win.
Driver and maker of [[see:La Jamais Contente]], nicknamed [[see:Le Diable Rouge]] for his red beard and record runs.
Nickname of [[see:Camille Jenatzy]], from the colour of his beard and his record-breaking runs.
Rival of [[see:Camille Jenatzy]]; the two staged publicity stunts to see who could build the fastest vehicle.
A tram-like railway that goes up a hill, from Latin [[from:funiculus]], thin rope; Rob finds it the most entertaining vehicle name.
Pedal-driven bicycles; the name means roughly speed feet.
Series of motorised rail cars built by the Rio Grande Southern Railway in the 1930s to carry passengers and mail.
Nickname for self-propelled, often gasoline-powered, rail cars that ran on short lines.
Nickname for tiny post-war European microcars such as the [[see:BMW Isetta]] and the [[see:Messerschmitt]] KR200.
An example of a [[see:bubble car]].
Name behind the KR200 [[see:bubble car]] and, probably, the fighter plane; it means knife smith.
A 1948 car with a centre-mounted headlight that looked cool.
Contrasted with [[see:automobile]], literally a self-mover.
British word for a [[equivalent:truck]], which Americans understand but don't use.
Probably from [[from:truckle]], a set of small wheels, hence also the railway [[see:bogie]]; Greek trochos, to run, is a less likely source.
The original word, a group of small wheels to help move something; its -le ending marks smallness, giving [[gave:truck]].
Example of the frequentative -le: to [[see:chuck]] often, cited when discussing [[see:truckle]].
The base of [[see:chuckle]].
Another -le word alongside [[see:spark]], given to illustrate [[see:truckle]].
The base of [[see:sparkle]].
Classic [[see:CB radio]] trucker phrase.
Film full of trucker slang, discussed in a previous episode.
Trucker slang for a cop on your tail; also [[equivalent:bear on your back end]].
Same as [[equivalent:bear on your donkey]]: police behind you.
Trucker slang for state troopers or highway patrol, who wore a Smokey Bear hat; this is why bears mean police.
Trucker slang for a parking ticket; paying it is [[see:feeding the bears]].
Trucker slang for paying a [[see:bear bite]], or ticket.
Trucker slang for a police helicopter, also [[equivalent:spy in the sky]].
Another trucker name for a police helicopter; see [[equivalent:bear in the air]].
Trucker slang for a boastful driver.
Trucker slang for someone who talks big on the radio because nobody knows where they are.
Slang for a slick little motorcycle.
Trucker slang for listening in on the radio without talking.
Trucker slang for roadkill.
Trucker slang for a piece of broken tyre left in the road.
Citizens band radio, used by citizens rather than police; mostly American, though British lads once used it like MSN Messenger.
[[see:CB radio]] code for receiving poorly.
[[see:CB radio]] code for okay, message received.
[[see:CB radio]] code for out of service.
[[see:CB radio]] code for in service.
[[see:CB radio]] code for repeat your message.
[[see:CB radio]] code for transmission completed, standing by.
[[see:CB radio]] code for location, shortened to 20, as in what's your 20; a [[see:home 20]] is where you live.
CB slang for where you live, from [[from:10-20]].
Compared with [[see:CB radio]], which British teenagers once used in a similar way to chat locally.
